title: Where a sensor stands
bodyMd:
An urban research group compares summer temperatures across neighbourhoods using sensors attached to municipal buildings. Its map shows the commercial centre as cooler than several residential districts. The researchers initially interpret the pattern as evidence that dense commercial development reduces heat. Before publishing, however, a technician notes that many central sensors sit beneath deep entrance canopies, whereas residential sensors are often mounted on exposed walls.

The group does not simply discard the original measurements. Those measurements accurately describe the microenvironments in which the sensors operated. The problem arises when a shaded doorway is treated as representative of all the streets around it. To investigate, the team installs additional sensors at standardized heights and exposure conditions and records pedestrian routes at fixed times. The revised measurements still reveal differences among neighbourhoods, but the original centre-versus-residential contrast becomes much smaller.

The researchers conclude that location within a neighbourhood is part of the measurement design, not an incidental detail to be documented after the analysis. Standardization makes some comparisons more defensible, but it also changes the question. A sensor in a standardized open location may be suitable for comparing exposed conditions while failing to describe the actual mixture of shade and sun encountered by pedestrians. The team therefore publishes both a standardized comparison and a route-based account, identifying the population of places and times each represents. Its revised claim is not that one map is universally correct and the other universally wrong, but that maps should be interpreted in relation to their sampling purposes.
